{{Quote|In the three and a half millennia since its introduction, it has become as traditional as its more formal cousin, which is now used almost exclusively in military and official capacities.|Milanda Vorgan on the Futhork|<ref name="TWW">{{Hyperspace|url=hyperspace/source/writtenword/index.html?page=1|text=The Written Word|int=The Written Word}}</ref>}}
'''Futhork''' was a style of traditional, handwritten [[Writing/Legends|calligraphy]] used by the [[Human/Legends|Human]] [[Naboo (people)/Legends|people]] of the [[Planet/Legends|planet]] [[Naboo/Legends|Naboo]]. This informal writing system had been developed in response to the [[Futhark/Legends|Futhark]]&mdash;the first Naboo alphabet, which derived from the [[Royal Script of Grizmallt|Royal Script]] of [[Grizmallt/Legends|Grizmallt]]. While Futhark was the official form, the reliance of all of its letters on ovals made it hard to read. This difficulty led to the creation of the more practical Futhork, during the [[Inter-Sith Wars period]].<ref name="TWW" /> The Futhork alphabet contained twenty-six characters,<ref name="CSWE">{{CSWECite|I|299|Futhork}}</ref> which were usually read from left to right. In that written form, words were distinguished by spaces.<ref name="E1VG">''[[Star Wars: Episode I: The Visual Dictionary]]''</ref>

In the height of the [[New Republic/Legends|New Republic]], the use of the Futhork alphabet was already three and a half [[Standard year/Legends|millennia]] old and was as traditional as the more formal Futhark, displacing it in every day and handwritten usage; the former was reduced in only formal and military context.<ref name="TWW" /> Ancient legends were written in this informal script, including the tale of [[Veré]] and [[Set]], two eternal lovers.<ref name="Max">{{DB|character|maxironagolerga|Agolerga, Pontifex Maxiron}}</ref> In the last decades of the [[Galactic Republic/Legends|Galactic Republic]], the art of writing in Futhork was still taught at school, and the six-year-old [[Ryoo Naberrie/Legends|Ryoo Naberrie]], niece of the famous [[Senator/Legends|Senator]] [[Padmé Amidala/Legends|Padmé Amidala]], was known to dislike this subject.<ref name="Ryoo">{{DB|character|ryoonaberrie|Naberrie, Ryoona}}</ref> At that time, even the farmers could write in both [[Aurebesh/Legends|Aurebesh]]&mdash;the most universal written form of the [[Galactic Basic Standard/Legends|Basic]] language&mdash;and Futhork fluently.<ref name="EG">{{StoryCite|story=End Game|book=Star Wars: Episode I The Phantom Menace (novelization)|bformatted=''Star Wars'': Episode I ''The Phantom Menace'' novelization, 2012 edition}}</ref>

The [[Professor/Legends|Associate Professor]] of [[Xenolinguistics]] [[Milanda Vorgan]] mentioned the Futhork in her paper "[[The Written Word: A Brief Introduction to the Writing Systems of Galactic Basic]]." In this work, Vorgan suggested that the Naboo had perhaps been loathe to adopt other writing systems in an effort to barrier themselves from the greater [[galactic community]]. However, she illustrated that they did use more widely embraced systems such as Aurebesh in the computer displays of their starships.<ref name="TWW" />

The wealthy citizens of Naboo sometimes wore embroidered [[Clothing/Legends|clothes]] ornated with Futhork calligraphy.<ref name="SW:DP">[[Darth Plagueis (novel)|''Darth Plagueis'']]</ref> In the same vein, some [[Engineer/Legends|engineers]] of the [[Theed Hangar/Legends|Theed Hangar]] like [[Simon Jabesq]] would label their duty [[Armor/Legends|helmet]] with their name in Futhork letters.<ref name="E1VG" />

==Behind the scenes==
Throughout various sources, the word "Futhork" has been spelled variously with<ref name="Max" /> or without an initial capital letter.<ref name="Ryoo" /> The present article follows ''[[The Complete Star Wars Encyclopedia]]'' in using the capitalized form.<ref name="CSWE" />

===Creation===
[[File:Futhork_concept.png|thumb|left|175px|Early concept art by Iain McCaig featuring the Futhork letters for A, B, C, D and F]]
The Futhork alphabet was created for the [[1999]] movie [[Star Wars: Episode I The Phantom Menace|''Star Wars'': Episode I ''The Phantom Menace'']]. It was developed as early as [[1997]] and was present in a drawing of Naboo helmets by concept artist [[Iain McCaig]].<ref name="E1:IG">[[Star Wars: Episode I Insider's Guide|''Star Wars'': Episode I ''Insider's Guide'']]</ref> In [[2000]], the passcodes screen of the [[LucasArts]] video game ''[[Star Wars: Episode I: Battle for Naboo]]'' featured all 26 letters, along with the question mark, the exclamation point and the ampersand.<ref name="SW:BFN">''[[Star Wars: Episode I: Battle for Naboo]]''</ref> As a result, the mapping of the Futhork alphabet was known from this point on, but the first official transliteration table was not published until [[2008]], with the release of ''The Complete Star Wars Encyclopedia''.<ref name="CSWE" />

In real life, [[Wikipedia:Futhork|Futhork]] was the name of a runic alphabet used in writing [[Wikipedia:North Germanic languages|North Germanic languages]] during the [[Wikipedia:Viking Age|Viking Age]]&mdash;a period spanning roughly the late 8th to 11th centuries.<ref name="Omni">{{WebCite|url=https://www.omniglot.com/writing/runic.htm|text=Runic alphabet|work=Omniglot|archivedate=20200804125506}}</ref>

===Examples in products===
The mapping of Aurebesh, the most universal and well-known ''Star Wars'' alphabet, was only inspired by the inscriptions found in the original movies, and those texts cannot be translated directly.<ref name="EchoStation">{{WebCite|url=http://www.echostation.com/features/aurebesh.htm|text=Aurebesh Soup&mdash;Recipe for a Star Wars Font Phenomenon|work=Echo Station|archivedate=20160520153232}}</ref> In the case of Futhork, a full symbol-to-letter correspondence seems to have been established from the beginning, since some readouts in this script can be transcribed into intelligible words. For example, the names "[[Iain]],"<ref name="E1:IG" /> "[[Simon Jabesq|Simon]],"<ref name="E1VG" /> and "[[Bernie Jabesq]]" appear on prop helmets.<ref name="E1:IG" /> However, most of the Futhork inscriptions seen in ''The Phantom Menace'' either read as gibberish or feature names of people who were part of the movie's production staff, including "[[Warren Fu]]."<ref name="TPM">{{Film|I}}</ref>

Likewise, in [[Star Wars: Episode I: The Visual Dictionary|''Star Wars: Episode I The Visual Dictionary'']], the instances of Futhork used in starship computer monitors only displayed either gibberish or jocular, out-of-universe statements such as "Yo Warren."<ref name="E1VG" /> Similarly, the 1999 interactive CD-ROM ''[[Star Wars: Episode I Insider's Guide]]'' contains private jokes and allusions such as "Franck Fu is the best."<ref name="E1:IG" /> In the roleplaying game guide ''[[Secrets of Naboo]]'', four brief Futhork inscriptions were included in the margins. However, they were used for decorative purpose only, and read as "impj," "thk," "uvqx," and "jti."<ref name="SoN">''[[Secrets of Naboo]]''</ref>

On the other hand, in [[Star Wars: Episode II Attack of the Clones|''Star Wars'': Episode II ''Attack of the Clones'']], the control panel of Senator Amidala's [[H-type Nubian yacht/Legends|H-type Nubian yacht]] featured readable writings in Futhork that made perfect sense in context. Among the readable words are the names of [[Obi-Wan Kenobi/Legends|Obi-Wan Kenobi]], [[Coruscant/Legends|Coruscant]], [[Geonosis/Legends|Geonosis]], and [[Tatooine/Legends|Tatooine]].<ref name="AOC">{{Film|II}}</ref>
